Best Practices

This guide defines the recommended architectural, testing, and extension patterns for building stable, deterministic applications with .

The practices in this document focus on predictability, lifecycle clarity, and deterministic execution across application code, integration tests, and framework environments. Each section builds on the core execution model of the and pipeline.

If you are new to , review the execution model first. If you are building production features or writing tests, use this page as a reference for stabilization patterns and lifecycle guarantees.

Architectural Ownership Boundaries
↑ top

Every must have a single architectural owner responsible for:

  • Pipeline configuration
  • State mutation
  • Lifecycle activation via initialize()
  • Public state exposure

A must never be partially configured at runtime. When it becomes accessible to consumers, its pipeline must already be fully defined and activated.

Once initialized, the pipeline becomes a closed, deterministic execution boundary. State cannot be altered outside of the pipeline, and no external system can mutate committed state directly.

All mutations must enter through the configured pipeline stages. As a result, execution ordering, side effects, and state commitment are fully controlled and observable. There are no hidden mutation paths, no reducer bypass, and no post-commit state alteration.

Pipeline Configuration Location
↑ top

A FeatureCell must fully configure its pipeline before exposing public state.

Angular

Pipeline configuration belongs in the owning service constructor. This ensures deterministic configuration and prevents partial initialization states.

  • Configure behaviors
  • Register filters and reducers
  • Call initialize()

React / Vue / Typescrpt

When using as pure TypeScript, configuration belongs at module scope during FeatureCell creation. The cell should be configured and initialized before being exported.

In all environments, configuration must occur before state consumption.

Service-to-FeatureCell Interaction Rule
↑ top

State mutation must occur through a single domain boundary. A should never be owned directly by UI components.

Note:

In all the patterns, the rule is identical: once initialized, the pipeline is the sole authority over state mutation. No component may bypass the pipeline or mutate state directly.

Examples
↑ top

In Angular applications, a must be owned and configured by a service. The service is responsible for:

  • Configuring behaviors and controllers
  • Calling initialize()
  • Issuing replaceState() and mergeState() mutations
  • Exposing read-only state to components

Components must never inject the Vault directly or invoke mutation APIs.

app.config.ts
// app.config.ts
export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [
    provideVault({ logLevel: 'off' }),

    provideFeatureCell(
      EmployeeService,
      {
        key: 'employees',
        initialState: []
      },
      [
        withArrayPushMergeBehavior
      ]
    )
  ]
};
employee.service.ts
// employee.service.ts
@FeatureCell<Employee[]>('employees')
@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class EmployeeService {

  private readonly vault = injectVault<Employee[]>(EmployeeService);

  constructor() {
    this.vault.initialize();
  }

  add(employee: Employee): void {
    this.vault.mergeState({
      value: [employee]
    });
  }

  readonly state = this.vault.state;
}

In React applications, the module that defines the acts as the architectural owner. Components must not call mutation APIs directly. Instead, they call exported domain functions. Components use useSyncExternalStore() to render the owning State.

employee.cell.ts
// employee.cell.ts
import { Vault, FeatureCell } from '/react';
import { withArrayPushMergeBehavior } from '/addons';

// 1️⃣ Initialize global runtime
Vault({ logLevel: 'off' });

// 2️⃣ Register FeatureCell
export const employeeCell = FeatureCell<Employee[]>(
  {
    key: 'employees',
    initialState: []
  },
  [
    withArrayPushMergeBehavior
  ]
);

// 3️⃣ Activate FeatureCell
employeeCell.initialize();

// 4️⃣ Domain-level mutation function
export function addEmployee(employee: Employee): void {
  employeeCell.mergeState({
    value: [employee]
  });
}

// 5️⃣ Export state surfaces
export const employeeState = employeeCell.state;
export const employeeState$ = employeeCell.state$;

Component Interaction Rule
↑ top

Components are consumers of state, not owners of state.

Components should:

  • Read state from an owning service (Angular)
  • Render State through useSyncExternalStore() (React)
  • Subscribe to exported state surfaces (Vue)
  • Trigger domain methods exposed by the owner

Components must not:

  • Call Vault mutation APIs directly
  • Configure pipeline behavior
  • Access pipeline stages

This separation guarantees clear responsibility boundaries, improved testability, and stable state lifecycles.

Examples
↑ top

In Angular applications, a must be owned and configured by a service. The service is responsible for:

  • Configuring behaviors and controllers
  • Calling initialize()
  • Issuing replaceState() and mergeState() mutations
  • Exposing read-only state to components

Components must never inject the Vault directly or invoke mutation APIs.

employee.component.ts
// employee.component.ts

import { Component, inject } from '@angular/core';
import { CommonModule } from '@angular/common';
import { EmployeeService } from './employee.service';

/**
 * UI component responsible for rendering FeatureCell state.
 *
 * This component consumes state exposed by EmployeeService.
 * It does not configure the pipeline and does not mutate state directly.
 */
@Component({
  selector: 'employee-view',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [CommonModule],
  template: `
    <div style="margin-bottom: 1rem;">
      <button (click)="addSample()">
        Add Sample Employees
      </button>
    </div>

    <!-- Value -->
    @if (state.hasValue()) {
      <div>
        <p>Employees: { { state.value() | json }}</p>
      </div>
    }

    <!-- Loading -->
    @if (state.isLoading()) {
      <div>
        Loading...
      </div>
    }

    <!-- Error -->
    @if (state.error()) {
      <div>
        Error: { { state.error()?.message }}
         
      </div>
    }
  `
})
export class EmployeeViewComponent {

  /**
   * Inject the domain service.
   * The service owns the FeatureCell and Vault pipeline.
   */
  private readonly service = inject(EmployeeService);

  /**
   * Read-only state surface exposed by the service.
   * This is a reactive StateSnapshotShape<T>.
   */
  readonly state = this.service.state;

  /**
   * Delegate mutation to the service.
   *
   * Architectural flow:
   * UI → Service → Vault → Pipeline → State Stage → Reactive UI update
   */
  addSample(): void {
    const sample = [
      { id: 11, name: 'Luke' },
      { id: 38, name: 'Leia' }
    ];

    this.service.add(sample);
  }
}

In React applications, the module that defines the acts as the architectural owner. Components must not call mutation APIs directly. Instead, they call exported domain functions.

EmployeeView.tsx
import { addEmployee, employeeCell } from './employee.cell';

export function EmployeeView() {
  const snapshot = employeeCell.useSyncExternalStore();

  function addSample() {
    addEmployee({ id: 11, name: 'Luke' });
    addEmployee({ id: 38, name: 'Leia' });
  }

  if (snapshot.isLoading) {
    return <p>Loading...</p>;
  }

  if (snapshot.error) {
    return <p role="alert">{snapshot.error.message}</p>;
  }

  const employees = snapshot.hasValue ? snapshot.value : [];

  return (
    <div>
      <button type="button" onClick={addSample}>
        Add Sample Employees
      </button>

      <pre>
        {JSON.stringify(employees, null, 2)}
      </pre>
    </div>
  );
}

In Vue applications, the module that defines the owns the state boundary. Vue components consume state and call exported domain functions — never the Vault directly.

EmployeeView.vue
<script setup lang="ts">
                      import { ref, onMounted, onUnmounted } from 'vue';
import { addEmployee, employeeState$ } from './employee.cell';

const employees = ref<Employee[]>([]);
let subscription: { unsubscribe(): void } | undefined;

onMounted(() => {
  subscription = employeeState$.subscribe(snapshot => {
    if (snapshot.hasValue) {
      employees.value = snapshot.value;
    }
  });
});

onUnmounted(() => {
  subscription?.unsubscribe();
});

function addSample() {
  addEmployee({ id: 11, name: 'Luke' });
  addEmployee({ id: 38, name: 'Leia' });
}
</script>

<template>
  <div>
    <button @click="addSample">
      Add Sample Employees
    </button>

    <pre>
      { { employees }}
    </pre>
  </div>
</template>

In pure TypeScript, the module that defines the acts as the owner. UI rendering is handled externally — the cell module exports domain functions and state surfaces only.

employee.view.ts
import { addEmployee, employeeState$ } from './employee.cell';
import type { Employee } from './employee.types';

// Subscribe to state changes
employeeState$.subscribe(snapshot => {
  if (snapshot.hasValue) {
    renderEmployees(snapshot.value);
  }
});

// Domain-level interaction
function addSample(): void {
  addEmployee({ id: 11, name: 'Luke' });
  addEmployee({ id: 38, name: 'Leia' });
}

function renderEmployees(employees: Employee[]): void {
  console.log(JSON.stringify(employees, null, 2));
}
Deterministic Initialization Guarantee
↑ top

does not require asynchronous pipeline configuration.

Because configuration is synchronous and execution is internally ordered, constructors and module-scope setup are safe initialization boundaries.

  • No deferred configuration patterns are recommended.
  • No lifecycle hooks are required for pipeline setup.
  • No partial initialization states should exist.

Once initialize() has been called, execution is deterministic and predictable across all supported environments.

State Mutation Discipline
↑ top

All state changes in must enter the pipeline through explicit update APIs.

State is never mutated directly. It is never modified in-place. It is never updated outside the pipeline.

Whether replacing state, merging partial updates, or streaming values over time, every update follows the same deterministic execution lifecycle:

  • Submit candidate value
  • Resolve and process deterministically
  • Commit a single immutable snapshot

Update APIs differ only in how candidate state is produced — not in how it is committed.

For complete API definitions and execution diagrams, see:

→ State Update APIs Documentation

Selecting an Update API
↑ top

Choose the update mechanism based on the structural intent of the change.

  • Use replaceState() when the incoming value is authoritative and should fully replace committed state.
  • Use mergeState() when applying partial or incremental updates.
  • Use fromStream() when state must react continuously to an external observable source.

Bridge APIs exist for migration scenarios but should not be the default choice in modern code.

In most cases, submit values directly to replaceState() or mergeState() for clarity and predictability.

Merge Strategy Discipline
↑ top

Merge semantics define how incoming values are structurally combined with committed state. Exactly one merge behavior may be active per .

Merge behaviors must define structural combination only. They must not encode business logic, validation rules, or conditional intent.

  • Merge defines structure, not meaning.
  • Reducers define meaning and transformation.
  • Filters define admission.
  • Merge never emits snapshots.

When selecting a merge behavior:

  • Use shallow or deep object merge when evolving structured state.
  • Use array append or push behaviors for additive collections.
  • Use replace semantics when arrays represent atomic snapshots.

Avoid embedding business rules inside merge logic. Structural combination should remain predictable and mechanical.

For detailed merge behavior documentation, see:

→ Merge Behaviors Documentation

Selecting a Merge Behavior
↑ top

defines exactly one active Merge behavior per . The Merge stage determines how the current committed state is structurally combined with a newly resolved incoming value.

Merge behaviors are purely structural. They do not perform business logic, validation, filtering, or policy evaluation. They define how values are combined, not why they change.

Timer & Async Stabilization
↑ top

Understanding stabilization boundaries is critical when integrating timers, asynchronous inputs, or external scheduling systems.

separates pipeline computation from state commitment. All state commitment occurs across a microtask boundary using queueMicrotask.

This guarantees:

  • Atomic state commitment
  • No partial snapshot visibility
  • Structural prevention of reentrancy
  • Deterministic observer notification ordering

However, when integrating with timers, policy schedulers, observables, external async systems, (or Angular effects), you must respect this stabilization boundary in both runtime and test environments.

If a mutation occurs, there is always a deterministic settlement boundary to await.

For the complete execution model, ordering guarantees, microtask commitment explanation, and async lifecycle semantics, see:

→ Read the Pipeline Execution Guarantees

Persistence & Encryption Discipline
↑ top

Persistence is an output-stage concern. It must never influence pipeline computation, state transitions, or mutation control flow.

In , persistence occurs strictly after a snapshot has been fully computed, reduced, and committed. Persist behaviors operate only on finalized pipeline output and are fail-safe by design.

  • Persistence must never mutate state.
  • Persistence must never affect pipeline success or failure.
  • Persistence must be treated as a durable side effect.
  • Persistence failures must never break FeatureCell execution.

When persistence is enabled, it should be configured at FeatureCell initialization time and treated as infrastructure—not as application logic.

For full implementation details, storage options, lifecycle diagrams, and behavior comparison tables, see:

→ Persist Behaviors Documentation

Data Security Boundary
↑ top

Browser storage mechanisms such as localStorage, sessionStorage, and document.cookie should be treated as plaintext by default.

Persisted FeatureCell state may contain user preferences, identifiers, or derived values. Without encryption, these values are readable at rest.

If persisted state contains sensitive or user-specific information, encryption should be enabled at the pipeline boundary.

  • Encryption operates only on persistence output.
  • In-memory state always remains plain and observable.
  • Encryption does not alter pipeline computation.
  • Decryption occurs during initialization before emission.

Encryption configuration must remain stable for the lifetime of stored data. Changing encryption parameters invalidates previously persisted values.

For full lifecycle guarantees, failure semantics, and configuration details, see:

→ Encrypt Behavior Documentation

Deterministic Testing & Verification
↑ top

Testing is a first-class architectural requirement in .

The serialized conductor queue, explicit microtask finalization boundary, and strict non-re-entrant execution model exist not only for runtime safety — but for deterministic verification under test.

Every execution layer is documented. Every stabilization boundary is explicit. The framework provides formal settlement guarantees through vaultSettled() and engine-level isolation tools.

If a mutation occurs, there is a deterministic boundary to await.

Architectural Smells
↑ top

The following patterns violate the deterministic execution model of and should be treated as architectural smells. While some may appear to function at runtime, they undermine ownership boundaries, execution guarantees, or immutability discipline.

These patterns should not appear in production code.

UI-Owned Mutation

Components must never call Vault mutation APIs directly. State mutation must pass through a single domain boundary owned by the owner (service or module).

  • Do not call replaceState() / mergeState() from UI components.
  • Do not inject the Vault into view-layer code.
  • Expose domain-level functions instead.

Business Logic Inside Merge

Merge behaviors define structural combination only. They must not encode validation rules, conditional intent, or business decisions.

  • Merge defines structure, not meaning.
  • Reducers define meaning and transformation.
  • Filters define admission policy.

Mutable Reducers

Reducers must never mutate existing state. Returning a mutated object violates snapshot immutability and breaks deterministic emission guarantees.

  • Always return new object or array instances.
  • Never modify properties on the incoming state reference.

Delayed or Conditional Initialization

A must be fully configured and initialized before being exposed to consumers. Delaying initialize() creates partial configuration states and undermines deterministic startup behavior.

  • Do not initialize inside lifecycle hooks unnecessarily.
  • Do not conditionally initialize based on runtime state.
  • Configure and activate synchronously.

Ignoring the Settlement Boundary in Tests

All state commitment occurs across a microtask boundary. Tests must respect this deterministic settlement boundary.

  • After a mutation, await settlement before asserting.
  • Use vaultSettled() or equivalent stabilization utilities.
  • Do not assert immediately after invoking mutation APIs.

Architectural discipline preserves determinism. When boundaries are respected, execution remains predictable, testable, and free from hidden mutation paths.
